meta.description: AI engineer building agents and machine learning systems that hold up in production, with a focus on reliability: evals, guardrails, calibrated uncertainty and observability.

person.name: Aashan Javed
person.role: AI Engineer, reliable agents in production
person.tagline: I build AI agents and machine learning systems that hold up in production, from data and models through evaluation, deployment and monitoring. My focus is reliability: agents that know when they're unsure, evals that predict real-world behaviour, and guardrails built in from the start. I enjoy finding exactly where a system breaks and engineering it until it can run on its own.

how_i_think.heading: Decide what the agent does when it's unsure before what it does when it's sure.
how_i_think.body: A support agent that answers every ticket will invent a refund policy for the tickets the help centre doesn't cover. So I give agents an explicit way out: escalate with a hand-off note, at a threshold calibrated on labelled cases for an error rate I chose up front. A failed model call is reported as an outage. Then I build the evals from the failures I actually find in the traces.

how_i_think.heading: Start with the simplest model that could work.
how_i_think.body: A logistic regression that ships beats a transformer that doesn't. Most 'model' problems turn out to be data problems: better features, cleaner labels, or being honest about what the data can't tell you. I reach for deep models when the simpler one has clearly plateaued, not before.

how_i_think.heading: A number without context isn't a result.
how_i_think.body: '+9% NDCG@5' only matters if I can tell you what baseline I'm beating, what split it's measured on, and what it would cost to be wrong. I try to write that down before I start training, not after, and I separate randomized-impression evaluation from logged-click evaluation, because position bias will quietly inflate everything otherwise.

how_i_think.heading: The hard part is rarely the model.
how_i_think.body: It's the pipeline that brings ERA5, Sentinel-2, and ground-truth into the same coordinate system without silently dropping rows. It's the inference path that's fast enough on the user's hardware. It's the drift detector that retrains the model before anyone notices the forecast went stale. I treat that work as the actual product.

projects.title: holdline: an Eval and Regression Gate for AI Agents
projects.tagline: Fails the pull request when a change makes an agent measurably worse, and checks the LLM judge before it is allowed to grade.
projects.problem: Agent changes ship on vibes: a prompt looks better on five examples, merges, and quietly breaks cases nobody re-ran. Checking only the final answer misses an agent that got there the wrong way, one run per case hides flaky behaviour, and the LLM judge doing the grading is rarely measured at all.

approach.data: Test cases as plain JSONL, or result files exported from any eval tool. Dogfooded on helpdesk-agent's 68 labelled support tickets, three runs each.
approach.models: Records every tool and model call, checks the path as well as the answer, runs each case several times and reports pass^k, compares before and after on the same cases with an exact McNemar test and a bootstrap interval, and measures an LLM judge against human labels: kappa, false-pass rate, and bias that flips between kinds of case.
approach.why: A merge decision is a yes or no, so the gate gives one with the reasons and the statistics behind it. Small test suites rarely prove a regression on their own, so must-pass cases and budgets sit next to the test.

results: On helpdesk-agent (68 tickets x 3 runs): 95.6% pass rate (95% CI 89.7 to 100), and every uncovered ticket escalated in all 66 runs
Caught a right answer citing the wrong article, and a correct answer that the grader marked wrong
Gated a cheaper setting: 0 cases broke, with 62% fewer model calls
Judge check runs in the browser, and its numbers match the Python package (tested)
projects.deployment: Open source (MIT) and on PyPI as holdline, with zero runtime dependencies. Command line, GitHub Action, single-file HTML reports and a browser judge check. 51 tests and CI on three Python versions.
projects.alt: A holdline report: the gate passed, pass rate with its interval, a case map of 68 cases and the cases that need attention

projects.title: helpdesk-agent: a Support Agent That Knows When to Escalate
projects.tagline: Replies only from the help centre, cites the article, and hands the ticket to a human with a note when it can't.
projects.problem: A chatbot with the help centre pasted in answers every ticket. On the tickets the help centre doesn't cover, it confidently invents policy: discounts, refunds, integrations that don't exist. In support, one invented policy costs more than ten escalations.

approach.data: A 30-article help centre for a fictional SaaS company and 68 labelled tickets: 46 answerable, with a gold answer and article, and 22 plausible tickets it does not cover. 27 tickets calibrate the threshold; 41 held-out tickets report the numbers.
approach.models: A bounded agent loop over a search tool: retrieve, then decide whether there is enough to reply, whether to search again with a reworded query, or whether to stop. It drafts several replies and uses their agreement as confidence. Split-conformal selective prediction sets the escalation threshold for a 10% error target, and output guards block any reply without a citation or whose key fact isn't in the cited article.
approach.why: Agreement across samples is a better confidence signal than the model's self-reported number, and a calibrated threshold turns 'how often may it be wrong' into a number I set.

results: Wrong replies on uncovered tickets: 0%, against 100% for a chatbot on the same model
Accuracy of the replies it sends: 96.4% (95% CI 88 to 100)
68.3% of tickets auto-resolved; the rest escalated with a hand-off note
Selective error 3.6% against a 10% target, on 41 held-out tickets
projects.deployment: Zero-dependency Python service on Render. The console shows a live ticket inbox with the agent's steps streaming as it works, a human queue for escalations, and an editable help centre that re-indexes on save. Rate limits, input guards, 62 tests and CI on every push.
projects.alt: helpdesk-agent console: a ticket resolved from a cited help-centre article

projects.title: Visual Research Assistant: Multimodal Agentic RAG
projects.tagline: Local-first agentic RAG over PDFs (text + tables + figures) with hallucination-aware retry.
projects.problem: Most 'chatbot over PDF' tools fall apart on real research papers: they ignore figures and tables, hallucinate citations, and lock you into cloud APIs. I wanted a multimodal agent that reasons over text, tables, and figures, runs locally on consumer GPUs, and tells you when it's wrong.

approach.data: Multi-page PDFs partitioned into text blocks, tables (preserved as HTML), and rasterized figures. Optional user-uploaded images for cross-modal queries.
approach.models: LangGraph state machine over five nodes: Router → Retriever → Generator → Critic → Finalize. Generator selects llava:7b for vision queries, llama3.2:1b for text. Critic is a separate model family with Pydantic-structured output for hallucination detection. ChromaDB + nomic-embed-text for retrieval.
approach.why: Cross-family critic so the judge isn't biased toward the generator's mistakes. Multi-vector retrieval (embed summaries, return originals) so semantic search doesn't truncate context. Retry only on hallucination; everything else surfaces on the first pass to keep latency honest.

results: 10-page PDF ingestion: 3–5 s
Text queries: 20–30 s
Image / cross-modal queries: 60–120 s (vision-bound)
Runs on 6 GB VRAM, ~7 GB total model disk
projects.deployment: Streamlit UI with citation badges and an agent-trace timeline. Docker Compose bundles Ollama + the app. SQLite checkpointer for resumable runs; structured JSON logs.
projects.alt: Visual Research Assistant agentic RAG interface

projects.title: Beijing Air-Quality Forecasting: MLOps Pipeline
projects.tagline: Drift-aware PM2.5 forecaster on a 9-point Beijing grid. Airflow + SageMaker + Evidently, end-to-end.
projects.problem: Most air-quality forecasting demos are static notebooks. The real problem is keeping a model fresh under drift (sensors fail, seasons shift, traffic patterns change) without manual retraining every week.

approach.data: Open-Meteo PM2.5 + weather across a 9-point grid over Beijing (39.75–40.05°N, 116.15–116.65°E); ~18,500 historical rows.
approach.models: XGBoost regressor (200 rounds, max_depth=6) with rush-hour, hour-of-day, and PM2.5 lag/rolling features. Recursive multi-step forecast for 1 h to 7 d horizons.
approach.why: XGBoost over deep models because the dataset size (~18.5K rows) and the operational requirement (drift-aware retraining every 6 h) make tabular gradient boosting the right tool. Save the deep model for when you have the data and the inference budget.

results: RMSE approval gate at 15.0 µg/m³ for production promotion
Drift-triggered retrain when >50% of features show PSI shift (Evidently AI)
End-to-end pipeline runs every 6 hours autonomously
projects.deployment: Airflow 2.10 orchestrates ingest → features → drift → conditional retrain. SageMaker training + Model Registry with RMSE-gated approval. FastAPI serves point, grid, and multi-day endpoints. Docker Compose on EC2 with Nginx + Postgres. Leaflet + Chart.js dashboard auto-refreshes every 5 min.

projects.title: Production Learning-to-Rank for Hotel Search
projects.tagline: LambdaMART + inverse propensity scoring on 9.9M Expedia rows. Beats the baseline ranker on every metric.
projects.problem: Hotel search ranking is fundamentally listwise: relevance is relative within each result set. And training on logged clicks just teaches the model to mimic the existing ranker, because position bias dominates the label signal.

approach.data: Expedia search data: 9.9M rows across 400K+ queries, of which 18,105 are randomized-impression queries that give unbiased ground truth.
approach.models: LightGBM LambdaMART over ~40 features (raw properties, match signals, Bayesian-smoothed historical engagement). Inverse Propensity Scoring with a power-law position-bias model: P(pos) = α · pos^(−β); reweight clicks by 1 / P(examine | position), capped at the 75th percentile.
approach.why: LambdaMART optimizes NDCG across full lists, matching the listwise objective. IPS is the cheapest credible answer to position bias, and it's measurable, because the randomization queries give a proper unbiased test set.

results: Wins on 30.9% of 59,903 test queries; ties on 37.4% (booked hotel already #1)
projects.deployment: Reproducible offline training and bias-corrected evaluation pipeline.

projects.title: AlphaEarth Climate Monitoring
projects.tagline: 10 m climate insights from coarse inputs using geospatial foundation embeddings.
projects.problem: Climate datasets like ERA5 are ≥1 km, too coarse to capture the neighborhood-scale heat, vegetation stress, or change patterns that real decisions depend on.

approach.data: Sentinel-2 + ERA5 / ERA5-Land via Google Earth Engine.
approach.models: Geospatial foundation embeddings + lightweight decoders for temperature prediction, similarity search, and change detection.
approach.why: One pretrained backbone serves multiple downstream tasks instead of training each from scratch, critical when imagery is multi-modal and labels are thin.

results: Output resolution: 10 m from ≥1 km inputs
Anomaly detection accuracy +17% vs baseline
projects.deployment: Earth Engine pipelines + Python; reproducible end-to-end with paper and code.

projects.title: Urban Data-Center Siting
projects.tagline: Multi-factor risk scoring for data center site selection using NASA EO data.
projects.problem: Data center siting is a multi-factor decision (climate risk, water, power, demographics) usually done in spreadsheets and consultancy reports: slow, opaque, hard to defend.

approach.data: NASA Earth Observation, OpenStreetMap, demographic and infrastructure layers.
approach.models: Composite scoring with multi-factor risk weighting, surfaced through an interactive comparison map.
approach.why: Decision-support tooling: interpretable scoring beats a black-box ranker when stakeholders need to defend the choice to legal and finance.

results: Multi-site comparison with real-time environmental analysis
Automated reports + interactive map UI
projects.deployment: React + Material-UI frontend, Flask API. Live demo videos.
projects.alt: Urban data center site assessment platform

projects.title: Revisitation-Aware Video Segmentation
projects.tagline: Stops static surfaces from being double-counted when AV routes loop.
projects.problem: When autonomous-driving datasets revisit the same street, static surfaces get counted multiple times, inflating composition statistics that downstream planning relies on.

approach.models: PSPNet semantic segmentation + temporal smoothing + per-pixel instance tracking + a semantics-driven revisitation detector.
approach.why: The bottleneck wasn't single-frame accuracy; it was temporal consistency. Cheaper to fix at the tracking layer than swap to a heavier transformer backbone.

results: mIoU +1.9
MOTA +15.3
ID switches −52%
Static overcount −50%

publications.title: How Fine Can Your Groups Get? The Breakdown of Plug-in Worst-Group Accuracy
publications.summary: Worst-group accuracy is the standard criterion for certifying group robustness, and it is almost always estimated by the plug-in minimum of per-group accuracies. That estimator's error is model-dependent: it vanishes when one group is clearly worst and is largest when group accuracies are near-tied. The bias therefore does not cancel when two models are compared, so a ranking can invert on the estimator alone.

publications.title: When Does a Frozen Time-Series Foundation Model's Uncertainty Fail, and What Actually Fixes It?
publications.summary: The natural rolling-origin implementation of this evaluation leaks its own future into calibration and overstates the apparent recovery, so every result is reported lagging feedback by the full horizon.
